ch21.note: Seymour Road (西摩路), a road in the western part of Shanghai's International Settlement, today Shaanxi North Road (陕西北路); it ran through a mixed residential and commercial district. Geographic; historical.

The pistol is a 马牌撸子 (here written 橹子), literally a “horse-brand pistol” — Chinese slang of the period for a Colt automatic. 马牌 (“horse brand”) names Colt after the rampant colt of its trademark; 撸子 is a northern colloquial word for a handgun. A Colt was a prized, high-end weapon, hence Zhongliang's remark. The reference is rendered plainly in the text. Corroborated.

ch21.anchor: singsong girl who knows nothing of a fallen nation's grief
ch21.note: An allusion to Du Mu (803–852), “Mooring on the Qinhuai” (泊秦淮): 商女不知亡国恨，隔江犹唱后庭花 — “The singsong girl knows not the grief of a fallen kingdom; across the river she still sings ‘Flowers of the Rear Courtyard.’” The “Rear Courtyard Flower” was the decadent air associated with the last, doomed ruler of the Chen dynasty, and Du Mu's couplet became the classic reproach of those who revel while their country falls. Here it fixes Su Lina's cover: the frivolous kept woman, singing while the nation burns. Literary allusion; the poet is historical.

Kagoshima Bay, at the southern tip of Kyushu, was chosen by the Imperial Japanese Navy in the autumn of 1941 to rehearse the attack on Pearl Harbor: its setting — a city on a small plain, ringed by mountains, on a shallow bay — closely resembled Honolulu and Pearl Harbor, and there the airmen perfected the shallow-water aerial torpedo the attack required. Father Brown, matching the terrain of Kagoshima to a map of Honolulu, has grasped what is coming. The scene falls before the raid of 8 December 1941 (7 December in Hawaii), with which the next installment opens. Historically corroborated.

ch22.note: Longhua (龙华; also romanized Lunghwa), in Shanghai's southern outskirts. After Pearl Harbor the Japanese interned Allied civilians at the Longhua Civil Assembly Centre, set up on the campus of a former middle school; it is the camp of J. G. Ballard's Empire of the Sun. Mass internment of enemy nationals began in earnest only in 1943, and the source telescopes it to December 1941, the day of the attack, when the first arrests of “hostile” foreigners did begin. Historical; the date is compressed. (Longhua was also, in the 1927–37 years, the site of the Nationalist garrison's execution ground — a different chapter of the same place.)

Bridge House (桥楼), beside the Sichuan Road bridge over Suzhou Creek, was the Shanghai headquarters and prison of the Kempeitai, the Japanese military police; foreigners and Chinese suspected of anti-Japanese activity were held there in caged cells and tortured, and it became a byword for horror. The real building was about eight stories; the source's “thirteen-story” is rendered as printed. Historical.
The Japanese soldier's word, 八格 in the source, transcribes baka (馬鹿, “fool, idiot”) — the opening of the common curse bakayarō (八格牙路, “damned fool”). Corroborated.

Sir Mark Aitchison Young (1886–1974), Governor of Hong Kong, surrendered the colony to Japan on 25 December 1941 — “Black Christmas” — after eighteen days of fighting. The Japanese surrender was received by Lieutenant General Sakai Takashi (酒井隆, 1887–1946), who had commanded the assault; Sakai was later tried and executed as a war criminal in 1946. Historical. (The fall of Hong Kong was noted earlier in The Rebel; the two men are named here.)

ch23.note: The Shōwa emperor, Hirohito, was born on 29 April 1901; his birthday, Tenchōsetsu (天長節), was a national holiday marked with gun salutes and celebration. On that day in 1942 he turned forty-one. Historical.

ch23.anchor: the second year of the Xuantong reign
ch23.note: Xuantong (宣统) was the reign title of Puyi, the last Qing emperor; its second year was 1910. The postmaster is saying he entered the postal service in 1910 — the year before the dynasty fell. Historical.

Renders 三教九流, literally “the three religions [Confucianism, Buddhism, Taoism] and the nine schools [of the classical philosophers]” — a set phrase for people of every kind and station, high and low. The literal catalogue is lost in the natural English. Idiom.

ch23.anchor: served two terms as a provincial governor under the Daoguang emperor
ch23.note: The office is the 巡抚 (xunfu), the chief civil administrator of a Qing province, here rendered “provincial governor.” The Daoguang reign ran 1821–1850. That the Japanese should desecrate the graves of a family with such a pedigree is the wound behind the postmaster's tears. Historical.

ch24.anchor: the First District of the Special Municipality of Shanghai
ch24.note: In the summer of 1943 the Japanese formally handed the International Settlement — the foreign-run concession — to Wang Jingwei's Nanjing government, which folded it into the Chinese-administered city; the source names the district it became. The retrocession was a propaganda gesture: real authority stayed with the Japanese and their puppet regime. Historical.

ch24.anchor: the Blue Sky, White Sun, and Wholly Red Earth flag
ch24.note: The national flag of the Republic of China (青天白日满地红) — a white sun on a blue canton, against a red field. Wang Jingwei's collaborationist government flew the same flag (at first with a small yellow pennant reading “Peace, Anti-Communism, National Reconstruction,” later dropped); its appearance over occupied Shanghai marks the puppet regime's authority, not a Nationalist one. Historical.

储备券, the banknotes of the Central Reserve Bank of Wang Jingwei's regime (the bank was noted earlier in The Rebel) — the paper money of occupied Shanghai. Wartime inflation steadily ate away their worth. Historical.

三炮台 was the Chinese name for Three Castles, a Virginia-tobacco brand of W. D. & H. O. Wills widely sold in Republican Shanghai; the Chinese name, literally “three gun-platforms,” renders the three castles of the English trademark. A premium foreign cigarette — the small luxury Su Lina leaves with each visit. Brand corroborated.

清乡 (qingxiang, “purifying the countryside”) was the joint Japanese and Wang-regime campaign, at its height from 1941, to wrest the rural districts around Shanghai from Communist and other resistance forces through blockade lines, household registration, and sweeps. The “winter plan” here is aimed at the New Fourth Army's base areas in central Jiangsu. Historical.

The shikumen (石库门, “stone-framed gate”) is the characteristic Shanghai lane-house: a row dwelling entered through a stone-framed doorway with heavy black wooden doors, opening off a communal alley. Material culture.

ch25.anchor: the warm nest of a pair of wild mandarin ducks
ch25.note: 野鸳鸯, literally “wild mandarin ducks.” Mandarin ducks (鸳鸯), which are believed to pair for life, are the Chinese emblem of wedded love; “wild” ones are a couple living together unwed, or illicitly. The image casts the safe-house as the nest of two who only pass as man and wife. Idiom and symbol.

ch25.anchor: Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, Central Executive Committee of the Chinese Nationalist Party
ch25.note: The card unmasks Qin Zhaokuan as an agent of the Zhongtong (中统) — the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Nationalist Party's Central Executive Committee, the intelligence organ of the CC Clique run by the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, established in its final form in 1938 and the party rival to Dai Li's military Juntong. The suave collaborator was a deep-cover Nationalist all along; the enameled Blue Sky, White Sun badge is the Nationalist party emblem, his token of identity. Historical.

ch25.anchor: take the two bullets he had caught for a self-inflicted ruse
ch25.note: 苦肉计, the “self-torture stratagem,” one of the classic Thirty-Six Stratagems: to wound oneself in order to win an enemy's trust. Qin means the Japanese will read his two wounds as a sacrifice he staged to prove his loyalty and clear himself of complicity. Idiom and allusion.

ch25.anchor: the dying sun was red as blood
ch25.note: The image echoes the closing line of Mao Zedong's lyric “Loushan Pass” (忆秦娥·娄山关, February 1935): 苍山如海，残阳如血 — “The blue mountains like a sea, the setting sun like blood.” That the memory of a dying Nationalist agent should carry a Communist poet's most famous image is a quiet irony of the book. Literary allusion; corroborated.

克鲁格.note: Father Kruger (克鲁格), the fair-haired German priest who succeeds Father Brown as the church's intelligence contact and later strikes his own bargain with Zhongliang. A fictional character; the source's transliteration of a German surname (Kruger/Krüger).

伊藤近二.note: The Japanese agent, planted as a postal inspector at the Jing'an office, who has lived twenty years in Shanghai and been exiled to it for defeatist talk. A fictional character; Japanese name in Hepburn romanization.

陈泰泞.note: The bald, self-effacing warehouse clerk at Shiliupu whom Qin Zhaokuan charges, in secret, with getting Su Lina safely out of Shanghai. A fictional character; pinyin.

原田.note: Mr. Harada (原田先生), the aged proprietor of the Japanese pawnshop on Fourth Avenue who keeps Qin Zhaokuan's sealed box against the day the ring appears. A fictional character; Japanese surname.

西摩路.note: A road in the western International Settlement, today Shaanxi North Road (陕西北路). Zhongliang keeps his cigarette stall at a corner off it.

桥楼.note: Bridge House (桥楼), by the Sichuan Road bridge over Suzhou Creek: the Shanghai headquarters and torture-prison of the Kempeitai. Historical.

鹿儿岛.note: City and bay at the southern tip of Kyushu, Japan, where the navy rehearsed the Pearl Harbor attack. Attested.

名古屋.note: City in central Japan; the exiled inspector Itō Kinji's home town. Attested.

虹口公园.note: The park in the Hongkou district (今鲁迅公园), in the Japanese quarter of Shanghai; Zhongliang's last safe-house stands near it.

十六铺.note: The old wharf district on the Huangpu in southern Shanghai (the source also prints the variant 十六浦). Site of the Longxin Warehouse where Chen Taining works.

抗日除奸队.note: 抗日除奸队, a resistance cell of the kind that hunted collaborators and turncoats in occupied Shanghai; here the unit to which Xiufen belongs. Rendered descriptively.

264旅.note: The Nationalist brigade of the 88th Division in which Su Lina's husband, Zhou Chukang, serves at the front.

鲶鱼.note: Zhongliang's code name after he takes over Zhou San's work (鲶鱼, “catfish”); he plays on it in English with Father Kruger.

储备券.note: 储备券, the banknotes of the Wang regime's Central Reserve Bank; the currency of occupied Shanghai.

三炮台.note: 三炮台, the Chinese name for the Wills brand Three Castles, a premium foreign cigarette of Republican Shanghai.

青天白日满地红.en: the Blue Sky, White Sun, and Wholly Red Earth flag
青天白日满地红.note: The national flag of the Republic of China, flown also by Wang Jingwei's collaborationist regime.

清乡.note: 清乡 (qingxiang), the Japanese and Wang-regime campaign to pacify and control the countryside around occupied Shanghai.

石库门.note: 石库门, the stone-framed-gate lane-house characteristic of Shanghai.

榻榻米.note: 榻榻米, the Japanese straw-mat flooring, fitting the safe-house in the Japanese residents' quarter.
